To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there exists an optimal curve for any given set of prescribed points and for any k ≥ 1; (2) there exists a unique optimal curve for k = 2; and (3) for any given curve, the corresponding optimal curve can be obtained as the unique solution of a linear system of equations.

• In the cubic case, we prove uniqueness of an optimal curve, • We prove existence of optimal curves in the general case, • We prove uniqueness in the cubic spline interpolation problem, • We provide an algorithm to construct optimal curves, and • We prove that optimal curves are unique for a certain class of curves.
• We prove the existence of an optimal solution for the general case.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following problems: 1.
the problem of best interpolation with free nodes, where the nodes are allowed vary freely.
the problem of finding a smooth curve through a set of prescribed data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the problem of best approximation of closed curves with free nodes by a given smoothness functional is a well posed one.
the problem of best interpolation with free nodes is well-posed.
for the cubic interpolation problem with free nodes, the unique solution is the closed cubic spline with free knots.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can construct optimal closed curves for any k and for any smoothness functional.
the problem of best interpolation with free nodes can be formulated as a constrained minimization problem of an energy functional with respect to the curve and its derivatives.
we have a constructive proof for the cubic case, and a constructive proof for existence for the general case, which is based on the cubic case.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optimal curves are not necessarily closed.
the optimal curve is a closed, piecewise algebraic curve.
the optimal curve is always a closed Bézier curve of degree 2k + 1, where the Bézier control points are determined by a set of linear equations.
